lessonTitle: Quality Improvement Methods: PDSA Cycles, Audit and Measurement

blocks.text: A ward sister notices that only about half of newly admitted patients have a falls risk assessment completed on the day they arrive. She could write an angry email, buy a new form, or ask a more useful question: 'What is one small change we could try tomorrow, and how will we know whether it helped?' That question is the heart of quality improvement.

blocks.markdown: Everyone who works in healthcare is expected to take part in improving care, not just delivering it. Three activities are easily confused: **quality improvement (QI)**, **clinical audit** and **research**. They share methods (data, measurement) but have different purposes. This unit teaches the **Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) cycle**, how to tell audit, QI and research apart, and how to choose **measures** that show whether a change has led to improvement.

blocks.title: Quality improvement
blocks.text: **Quality improvement** is a systematic, data-driven approach in which people closest to the problem test changes in their own setting to improve outcomes, patient experience and system performance. It typically uses small, rapid tests of change and repeated measurement over time.

blocks.markdown:
### The PDSA cycle

The PDSA cycle, associated with W. Edwards Deming and widely used in the NHS Model for Improvement, is a way to test a change on a small scale and learn quickly. Rather than rolling out a large change and hoping, you run many short cycles, each building on what the last one taught.

The **Model for Improvement** begins with three questions: *What are we trying to accomplish? How will we know that a change is an improvement? What change can we make that will result in improvement?* The PDSA cycle then tests the change.

blocks.caption: The four stages of a PDSA cycle
rows: What will we test, and what do we predict?
State the objective, the change, who, when and where, and the prediction; decide what data to collect
Carry out the test on a small scale and record observations, including problems
Compare the data with the prediction; consider what went well and what surprised you
Adopt, adapt or abandon the change, and plan the next cycle

blocks.title: A PDSA cycle for a ward problem
blocks.prompt: On a ward, 22 of 40 consecutive admissions (55%) had a falls risk assessment completed within 24 hours. The team's aim is to raise this to at least 90% within 8 weeks. They propose adding a reminder line to the admission checklist. Describe the first PDSA cycle.

steps.text: Plan: aim and prediction. Test the reminder line on one bay, for one week, with a single named nurse leading. Prediction: at least 80% of admissions to that bay will have an assessment within 24 hours. Data to collect: number of admissions and number with a completed assessment.
Do: run the test. Record what happens, including that two admissions arrived at night when the form was not available.

Study: in the week there were 10 admissions to the bay and 7 had a completed assessment, so 7/10 = 70%. This was below the prediction of 80% but higher than the 55% baseline. Night-time forms were a barrier.
Act: adapt rather than abandon. Add forms to the night admission pack and re-test in the same bay for another week before spreading to other bays.

blocks.answer: The first cycle gave 70% against a prediction of 80% and identified a barrier, so the team adapted the change and ran a second small test.

blocks.title: Start small, learn fast
blocks.text: PDSA works because failure is cheap. A change tested with one nurse and one bay for one week costs little and yields information. Scaling up happens only after repeated cycles show the change works in different conditions.

blocks.markdown:
### Clinical audit, quality improvement and research

All three use data, but they differ in **purpose** and **governance**.

- **Clinical audit** asks 'Are we doing what we should be doing?' by comparing current practice with an agreed **standard** (for example a guideline), then, if standards are not met, making changes and **re-auditing** to complete the cycle.
- **Quality improvement** asks 'How can we do it better?' by testing changes iteratively, often when no ready-made standard exists or the way to meet it is unknown.
- **Research** asks 'What is the right thing to do?' by generating new, **generalisable knowledge**, usually with a defined protocol, and in the UK requires appropriate approval (for example from a research ethics committee and the Health Research Authority).

blocks.caption: Audit, QI and research compared
rows: Are we meeting a known standard?
How can we improve this process?
What is the best treatment or explanation?
Repeated PDSA cycles of small changes
Formal protocol, often with randomisation or controls
May involve allocation or extra procedures

blocks.title: Which is it?
blocks.prompt: Classify each project: (1) Check whether 100 consecutive discharge letters meet the hospital's standard that they are sent within 48 hours. (2) Test whether a daily 5-minute huddle reduces the number of patients waiting for pharmacy supplies on discharge, adjusting the huddle each week. (3) Randomly allocate patients on two wards to a new nutrition protocol or usual care to see if it reduces length of stay across hospitals.

steps.text: Project 1 compares practice with a defined standard (48 hours) and would be followed by action and re-audit: clinical audit.
Project 2 tests a change, adjusting it each cycle in response to data, to improve a local process: quality improvement.
Project 3 randomly allocates patients to test a hypothesis and aims for generalisable knowledge: research, which needs research approvals and consent.

blocks.answer: 1 is clinical audit, 2 is quality improvement, 3 is research.

blocks.markdown:
### Choosing measures

To know whether a change is an improvement you must measure. The Model for Improvement uses three families of measure:

- **Outcome measures** show the result for patients (for example the percentage of patients with a falls assessment completed is a process; falls per 1000 bed-days is an outcome).
- **Process measures** show whether the steps we changed are being done.
- **Balancing measures** look for unintended consequences elsewhere (for example whether the extra form delays admission, or increases staff overtime).

Good measures are clearly defined (numerator and denominator stated), collected regularly, and **plotted over time** on a run chart so that real change can be distinguished from random variation. A single before-and-after comparison is weak evidence. Use **rates or percentages** rather than raw counts when the number of patients changes from week to week.

blocks.caption: Measures for a falls-reduction project
rows: Percentage of admissions with a risk assessment within 24 hours
Whether the changed process is happening
Average time from arrival on ward to first nursing assessment completed
Whether the new process creates delay elsewhere

blocks.caption: Percentage compliance, the basic calculation in audit and process measurement.

points: A PDSA cycle tests a change on a small scale: Plan (with a prediction), Do, Study the data, Act to adopt, adapt or abandon, then repeat.
Clinical audit compares practice with a standard and re-audits; QI tests changes iteratively to improve a process; research creates generalisable knowledge and needs ethical approval.
Use outcome, process and balancing measures, defined as percentages or rates and plotted over time, to show whether a change has led to real improvement.

questions.stem: In a PDSA cycle, a team has run a one-week test of a new patient identification prompt and now compares the data with their prediction. Which stage is this?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: Study compares results with predictions and records learning.
distractorRationale.b: Plan is before the test, when the prediction is made.
distractorRationale.c: Do is running the test itself.
distractorRationale.d: Act is the decision to adopt, adapt or abandon after studying.

questions.explanation: After the change has been tested (Do), the Study stage analyses what happened against what was predicted. The Act stage then decides what to do next.

questions.stem: A doctor checks 60 consecutive records to see whether each patient with suspected sepsis received antibiotics within the time set in a local guideline, and plans to repeat the check in six months. How should this project be classified?

options.text: A PDSA cycle with no standard

distractorRationale.a: Correct: compares practice with a defined standard and plans a re-audit.
distractorRationale.b: It does not aim to create new generalisable knowledge.
distractorRationale.d: A defined standard is being used, so it is audit rather than a test of change.

questions.explanation: Audit compares current practice with an established standard and re-measures after action. This project has a standard (the guideline time), a sample and a planned re-audit.

questions.stem: A team wants to reduce delays in discharge medication supply and tests a change in one bay. Which would be the best balancing measure?

options.text: Pharmacy staff overtime hours or other new delays elsewhere in the discharge process
Percentage of patients receiving medication on time
Number of patients discharged in the bay
The team's enthusiasm for the project

questions.correctOptionText: Pharmacy staff overtime hours or other new delays elsewhere in the discharge process

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a balancing measure looks for unintended consequences in other parts of the system.
distractorRationale.b: That is a process or outcome measure of the target itself.
distractorRationale.c: A raw count of discharges does not check for harm elsewhere.
distractorRationale.d: Enthusiasm is not an objective measure.

questions.explanation: Balancing measures check that an improvement in one area is not causing problems elsewhere. Here, extra workload or delays in pharmacy would be an unintended consequence.

questions.stem: Which statement best identifies the difference between quality improvement and research?

options.text: QI tests changes to improve a local process, using iterative cycles, whereas research aims to generate generalisable new knowledge, usually with a formal protocol and ethical approval
QI never uses data, whereas research always does
QI always requires randomisation, whereas research does not
There is no difference; the terms are interchangeable

questions.correctOptionText: QI tests changes to improve a local process, using iterative cycles, whereas research aims to generate generalisable new knowledge, usually with a formal protocol and ethical approval

distractorRationale.c: Randomisation is a research design feature, not a QI requirement.
distractorRationale.d: They have distinct purposes and governance.

questions.explanation: QI is aimed at improving a local process through repeated small tests and measurement, while research seeks generalisable knowledge and needs formal approvals. Both use data but with different goals and governance.

questions.stem: True or false: a single before-and-after comparison of two numbers is the strongest way to show a QI change has worked.
questions.explanation: Two data points cannot distinguish a real change from natural variation, so measures should be collected regularly and plotted over time, for example on a run chart. Repeated measurements make patterns and shifts visible.

questions.stem: In an audit of 80 consecutive patients on a medical ward, 56 had their pain score documented at admission, as required by the standard. Calculate the percentage compliance with the standard.
questions.explanation: Compliance is the number meeting the standard divided by the number audited, times 100, so 56 / 80 x 100 = 70%. Stating a numerator and denominator makes the measure clear and repeatable.

questions.stem: At baseline, a ward gave oral nutrition screening to 24 of 60 admissions. After three PDSA cycles, 45 of 60 admissions were screened. By how many percentage points did the process measure improve?
questions.explanation: Baseline compliance was 24/60 = 40% and after the cycles it was 45/60 = 75%, so the improvement is 75 - 40 = 35 percentage points. Using percentages allows comparison even if the number of admissions changes.

questions.stem: A student nurse notes that patients on a ward often wait more than 20 minutes for help to reach the toilet after pressing the call bell. Outline a first PDSA cycle to test a change, giving the Plan, Do, Study and Act stages.
markingGuide: Plan: states a clear aim and a small change to test, such as a scheduled 'comfort round' every two hours, with a prediction and who, where and when
Plan: identifies a measure, such as time to respond or percentage of calls answered within a defined time, and how data will be collected
Do: tests on a small scale, for example one bay for one week, and records problems
Study: compares the data with the prediction and notes what was learned or unexpected
Act: adopt, adapt or abandon the change and plan the next cycle
Mentions starting small and repeating cycles
questions.explanation: The key features of a PDSA cycle are a prediction, small-scale testing, and learning that shapes the next cycle. Defining a measure in advance allows the Study stage to be objective.

questions.stem: Distinguish clinical audit, quality improvement and research, with a brief example of each from a ward setting.
markingGuide: Audit: compares practice with an agreed standard, then acts and re-audits; example such as checking compliance with a guideline
QI: iterative testing of changes to improve a local process using PDSA and measurement over time; example such as testing a ward huddle
Research: aims to generate generalisable new knowledge with a protocol and ethical approval; example such as a randomised comparison of two treatments
Notes that all three use data but differ in purpose and governance
Mentions that audit and QI usually use routine data and local governance while research needs ethics approval
questions.explanation: Purpose is the key discriminator: checking against a standard, improving a process or discovering new knowledge. Recognising the type guides the correct approvals and methods.

questions.stem: A hospital introduces a new checklist to reduce delays in the removal of urinary catheters. Propose one outcome measure, one process measure and one balancing measure, and explain how you would display the data to judge whether the change is an improvement.
markingGuide: Outcome measure: for example the rate of catheter-associated urinary infections per 1000 catheter-days, or average catheter duration in days
Process measure: for example the percentage of catheters with a documented daily review or removal on the planned day
Balancing measure: for example the rate of re-catheterisation or additional nursing time required
Each measure defined with numerator and denominator and collected regularly
Plots data over time, for example a run chart with the date of the change marked, rather than a single before and after comparison
Explains that sustained shifts or trends beyond random variation indicate a real change
questions.explanation: A complete measurement plan covers results, the steps changed, and possible harm elsewhere. Plotting data over time lets the team separate genuine improvement from normal variation.
